newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Poihipi power plant to cut Mercury's costs - paper.
newsitem.headline: Poihipi power plant to cut Mercury's costs - paper.

text.p: Mercury Energy's cost of electricity is expected to drop when it fires up its Poihipi geothermal power plant in around three weeks, the New Zealand Herald reported on Friday.
The plant is in the process of being recommissioned, after local Maori opponents earlier this week dropped their opposition to air discharge permits being granted for the facility.

Mercury generation project engineer Minoru Frederiksens said initial production would be about 16 hours a day but it was planned to move to 24-hour operation. The plant is designed to produce 55 megawatts of electricity, enough to supply about

The power station is a joint venture between Mercury, which holds 51 percent, and the McLachlan family, of Taupo. It has been mothballed since December, awaiting the outcome of hearings over air discharge permits.

The NZ$78 million power station is drawing geothermal energy from the Wairakei field and was the first privately owned project to be issued a geothermal energy licence for commercial power generation since the Electricity Corporation gained its generation monopoly.

Frederiksens noted that once Poihipi is fully commissioned Mercury will be 35 percent self-sufficient in electricity supply. The company's other main generation plant is the recently commissioned gas-fired Southdown project in Penrose.
Mercury also is building, in association with Fletcher Challenge and TransAlta of Calgary, a 350 megawatt power station at Stratford.
Frederiksens said that once the Stratford plant was commissioned next year Mercury would be producing 55 percent of the power it sells.
Analysts estimate Mercury will save up to 20 to 25 percent by generating its own power rather than purchasing on the wholesale market.
However, those savings will be offset by the actual costs of establishing the generation plant.

If Mercury decides to build further generation plants then it might share the costs with Power New Zealand, which is its competitor in the Auckland market. Mercury and Utilicorp NZ, a subsidiary of UtiliCorp of the United States, this week formed a joint venture that will have a controlling stake in Power NZ.
